title: Programmed I/O: The Polling Loop and What It Costs
quickIdea: In programmed I/O the CPU moves every word itself and sits in a loop asking the status register whether the device is ready. The cost is the waiting, and it is a simple product: polls per second times the time each poll takes.
remember: Per word the CPU does: read the status register, test the ready bit, read the data register, store the word to memory. The device never touches memory.
The wait is busy waiting: the CPU is executing the loop, so the time is spent, not saved.
Polling cost per second = (polls per second) x (time per poll). As a fraction of the second, that is the CPU utilisation the device consumes.
Cost per second including the transfer = polls per second x time per poll + events per second x time per event.
Programmed I/O is the right choice for a rarely-ready slow device only when the wait is genuinely short or the CPU has nothing else to do; otherwise it is pure waste.

example.prompt: A keyboard is used at 1 keystroke per second. The system polls it every 10 ms and each poll costs 100 us; when a keystroke is found, 200 us more are spent processing it. What fraction of a second does polling consume?
example.work: Polls per second = 1 s / 10 ms = 100. Polling time = 100 x 100 us = 10,000 us = 10 ms. Processing happens once per second, because there is one keystroke: 200 us. Total = 10,200 us = 0.0102 s.
example.answer: 0.0102 of each second, that is 1.02% of the CPU, for a device that produces one character per second.

gateAngle: This is the numerator of GATE CSE 2023 Q.34. The exam keeps the arithmetic deliberately simple and hides the difficulty in the counting: how many polls in a second, and how many times the processing cost is paid. The other classic use is a comparison against the interrupt scheme on the same device.

variations.label: VERIFIED PYQ
variations.question: GATE CSE 2023 Q.34: the polling fraction is 0.0102 and the interrupt fraction is 0.001 for the same keyboard. What is their ratio?
variations.why: 0.0102 / 0.001 = 10.2; the interrupt scheme spends a tenth of the time because it pays only per event.

variations.label: PREDICTED VARIATION
variations.question: The same keyboard, but polled every 1 ms instead of every 10 ms. What is the polling fraction now, and what does it tell you?
variations.answer: 1000 polls x 100 us = 100,000 us = 0.1 s, plus 200 us for the keystroke: 0.1002. Polling ten times more often costs ten times more CPU for exactly the same one character per second.
variations.why: It shows that polling cost is set by the poll rate, not by the data rate - the defect the interrupt scheme removes.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: A device produces one byte every 100 us and the CPU polls it every 100 us with a 20 us poll. Is polling reasonable here?
variations.answer: No: 20 us out of every 100 us is 20% of the CPU, and the device is producing data at exactly the rate the CPU is checking, so the CPU is spending a fifth of its life on a device that is never idle. An interrupt, or DMA, is clearly better.
variations.why: Polling looks acceptable only when the poll interval is long compared with the event interval.

trap.what: Charging the per-event processing time on every poll instead of once per event.
trap.why: Processing happens only when a poll actually finds data. With one keystroke per second and 100 polls per second, 99 polls find nothing and pay only the poll cost.
trap.counterexample: Using 200 us per poll gives 100 x 300 us = 30 ms, three times the correct 10.2 ms. The ratio against the interrupt scheme then comes out at 30 instead of 10.2.

check.question: A system polls 100 times per second at 50 us per poll and nothing else is spent. What fraction of the CPU does polling take?
check.answer: 100 x 50 us = 5000 us = 5 ms, so 0.005 of the CPU, or 0.5%.
check.explanation: Multiply, then convert to a fraction of one second. The same arithmetic with 100 us per poll gives 1%.
